title: Sampling Bias Simulator
summary: A generated population of 4,000 fictional students whose true mean is known, three recruitment methods and repeated draws. The teaching target is the difference between an estimate that scatters and an estimate that is systematically off.
learningObjectives: Distinguish sampling variability from selection bias, and say which one a larger sample fixes.
Explain why a convenience sample is worst when ease of reach is related to the outcome.
Explain why a quota corrects the composition of the quota variable and nothing else.
Predict what changing the sample size does to the spread of estimates and what it does not do to their centre.
Recognise that an unbiased method is not made more unbiased by being larger.
interactionTypes: repeated simulated recruitment from a fixed population
live histogram of estimates against the true population mean
recruitment method, sample size and seed as separate controls
three headline figures separating centre from spread
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The figure marks the population mean with a labelled line and states in its description how many studies were run, by which method, with what sample size, where the estimates centred and how far that is from the truth. Every plotted quantity also appears as a headline figure in text, so nothing depends on reading bar heights. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated. The population of 4,000 students is generated once from a fixed seed and its mean is computed from the generated population rather than asserted, so it is exactly what a perfect census would return. No real student, institution or survey is represented.
simulationNotes: Weekly independent study hours are 12.6 plus 0.6 for second years and 1.4 for third years, minus 2.2 for commuters and 3.0 for students with jobs, plus Normal(0, 4), clamped at zero. Recruitment is weighted sampling without replacement by the exponential-race method, with weight 1 for everybody giving a simple random sample. The convenience weights make commuters and students with jobs much less likely to be reached and make the chance of being reached rise with the persons own study hours, which is selection on the outcome itself. Quota sampling fills equal numbers per year of study by the same convenience weights within each year. The selection weights are invented and were chosen to make the effect legible rather than to estimate how much more likely a commuter is to be in a library.
readmeTopic: sampling bias, sampling variability, and which one a larger sample fixes
